title: A 2% annual wealth tax above £10 million
headline: Contested. 2% above £10m from 2030-31: up to £24bn, or £18.5bn with more avoidance.
description: The campaign proposal backed by Tax Justice UK and Patriotic Millionaires: 2% a year on net wealth above £10 million, paid by about 0.03% of people. Its "up to £24 billion" rests on the Wealth Tax Commission’s low-avoidance assumption, that reported wealth falls 14% for each point of tax. Tax Policy Associates re-ran it on the Commission’s high-avoidance case, 34%, and got £18.5 billion; that is the figure scored here, held flat in cash. Nobody in government has costed it, and the two sides disagree about whether the people would stay.

baselinePolicy.text: The UK has no annual wealth tax. Wealth is taxed when it changes hands (capital gains tax, inheritance tax, stamp duties) and through council tax on homes.
alreadyIncludes: Nothing: no annual wealth tax exists or is planned.

earliestStart.text: An annual wealth tax needs its own Act, a valuation regime and new HMRC systems, and is paid the January after the tax year. Tax Policy Associates expects it to apply first in 2029-30 and pay in January 2031: nothing before 2030-31.

sources.quote: the tax would first apply in the 2029/30 tax year, with the first revenue received in January 2031
could take a total of four years from inception to full operation

terms.label: Tax Policy Associates’ re-run of the 2% above £10m proposal on the Wealth Tax Commission’s high-avoidance (34%) case

source.quote: if the 34% figure was used then the revenue raised would be significantly less – £18.5bn

rawSource.note: The cautious published figure: TPA’s £18.5bn on the high-avoidance case, held flat in cash from the start year. The campaign’s £24bn (low-avoidance case, Advani) is named on the card and not scored. Nothing is counted before 2030-31: see earliestStart.

caveats: Two published figures for one tax: up to £24 billion with a 14% behavioural response, £18.5 billion with 34%. Both come from the same Wealth Tax Commission machinery and neither has been certified; the OBR would form its own view. This card takes the lower one.
Annual, on about 32,000 people, and concentrated: TPA says 80% of the yield comes from about 5,000 people and about 15% from ten. A handful leaving or revaluing removes billions.
Valuation of private businesses, land and art is the administrative problem; the Commission itself recommended a one-off tax rather than an annual one.

considerations.text: The whole argument is here. The campaign assumes 14% of wealth disappears from the base per point of tax; TPA says 34% is plausible and the yield falls to £18.5 billion, with £500 billion of wealth leaving or moving into hard-to-value assets. This card already takes the harsher case; the OBR could go further.

sources.quote: The proponents use the 14% figure without any justification
This figure includes behavioural response, calculated by Arun Advani.

considerations.text: Only people with more than £10 million of net wealth pay, 0.03% of the population by Tax Justice UK’s count; polling it cites finds three quarters of the public in favour.
Neither HMRC nor the ONS publishes a wealth base above £10 million. TPA notes HMRC would need returns from perhaps 16,000 more people with wealth near the threshold to police it.

sources.quote: around 32,000 taxpayers would pay the tax

interactions.text: Two wealth taxes on the same £10 million threshold. Pick one design: 1% on the Commission’s figures or 2% on the campaign’s.
